Cashmere is an exceptionally soft, fine, and warm fiber — and the fabric made from it — that comes from a specific type of goat called the cashmere goat (also known as the Pashmina goat).

Cashmere goats live in harsh, high-altitude, cold climates — primarily in regions like Mongolia, Inner Mongolia (China), Kashmir (India/Pakistan), Afghanistan, and parts of Central Asia. To survive the brutal winters there, these goats grow a special inner coat of ultra-fine, downy hair beneath their coarser outer fur. This inner layer is what cashmere is.

The fiber is collected — usually by combing the goat, not shearing it — once a year in spring, when the goat naturally sheds its winter undercoat. One goat produces only about 150–200 grams of usable fiber per year, which is very little. That's why cashmere is rare and expensive.
What makes cashmere different from regular wool

Regular wool comes from sheep. It is functional and warm, but the fibers are thicker and can feel rough or scratchy against the skin.

Cashmere fibers are much finer — far thinner in diameter than sheep's wool. This extreme fineness is what gives cashmere its defining qualities:

  • Softness — It feels incredibly smooth and gentle against the skin. Even people who find regular wool itchy can usually wear cashmere comfortably.
  • Lightweight warmth — Cashmere is roughly 8 times warmer than sheep's wool by weight. So a thin cashmere sweater can keep you just as warm as a much bulkier wool one.
  • Breathability — It regulates temperature naturally, keeping you warm in cold weather and not uncomfortably hot indoors.
  • Luxurious drape — Cashmere fabric hangs and flows beautifully on the body. It doesn't stiffen like cheaper materials.
What cashmere looks like as a material

As a raw fiber, cashmere is a fine, soft, often whitish or grey down. Once processed, it becomes yarn, which is then knitted or woven into fabric. The finished fabric has a very smooth, almost silky surface with a subtle loft (a slight fluffiness). Over time and with use, cashmere can develop pilling — tiny balls of fiber on the surface — which is a natural characteristic of the material, especially lower-grade cashmere.

Not all cashmere is equal. The quality is mainly determined by the fineness (diameter) and length of the fibers:

  • Finer and longer fibers → softer, stronger, more durable, and more expensive.
  • Coarser or shorter fibers → cheaper to produce but less soft and more prone to pilling.

High-quality cashmere is graded as Grade A (the finest and softest) down to Grade C (coarser, lower quality). A lot of cheap "cashmere" products in the market use low-grade or blended cashmere, so the price and brand matter.

Because it is warm, light, and soft, cashmere is mostly used in clothing items that sit close to the skin:

  • Sweaters and jumpers — the most common use
  • Cardigans and hoodies
  • Scarves, wraps, and shawls — especially popular because even a thin cashmere scarf is very warm
  • Gloves and hats
  • Socks and base layers
  • Blankets and throws

Cashmere garments are considered luxury items and are associated with high fashion and quality craftsmanship. Brands like Loro Piana, Brunello Cucinelli, and others have built reputations specifically around premium cashmere.

Because the fibers are so fine and delicate, cashmere requires gentle care:

  • It should ideally be hand-washed in cold water with a mild detergent, or dry-cleaned.
  • It should never be wrung out or tumble-dried, as heat and agitation cause the fibers to shrink and felt (mat together permanently).
  • It should be laid flat to dry, not hung — hanging stretches it out of shape.
  • When stored, it should be folded, not hung on a hanger.
  • Cedar balls or lavender sachets are used near stored cashmere to repel moths, which are attracted to natural animal fibers.

With proper care, a good cashmere garment can last decades.

The price comes down to a few compounding factors:

  1. Scarcity — Each goat yields very little usable fiber per year.
  2. Labor-intensive collection — The fine undercoat must be carefully combed out by hand.
  3. Processing — Separating the fine inner fibers from the coarser outer guard hairs requires skilled work.
  4. Geographic concentration — Most of the best cashmere comes from remote, specific regions with limited output.
  5. High demand — It is universally recognized as a premium material.

A genuinely high-quality cashmere sweater can cost anywhere from $150 to over $1,000, depending on the grade and brand.

When people say something is made of cashmere, they mean it is made from this fine goat fiber — and the word carries a strong connotation of luxury, softness, warmth, and quality. It is the gold standard of warm, wearable textiles. Calling something "the cashmere of [anything]" in conversation means it is the finest, most premium version of that thing.
